issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Benchmark the BF16 kernels and fusions in [OLMo-core 3](https://allenai.org/papers/olmocore3) against Marin's current Grug MoE path to find small changes that improve training throughput. Start with candidates that preserve the current BF16 precision, routing, and optimizer behavior. MXFP8 training adoption remains deferred over stability concerns.

Use OLMo-core revision [`a800c06`](https://github.com/allenai/olmo-core/tree/a800c06edcec8e4652de2f80fe0ea572d689fcc3) as the source reference. Use the resolved [GB200 Hero recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/hero_recipe.py) to define baseline shapes and settings. Profile and rank:

- Grouped expert GEMMs: compare forward, activation-gradient, and weight-gradient legs on GB200 at Hero's actual latent dimensions, rows per expert, and uneven group sizes. Include the complete expert MLP forward/backward boundary and any conversion or layout costs.
- Activation, weighting, and buffer fusions: inspect SwiGLU forward/backward, route-weight application, and dispatch/combine staging copies. Benchmark opportunities that remove an intermediate allocation or memory pass after checking what our current kernels already fuse.
- Shared-expert compute packing: compare the current separate shared MLP calls with packed projections or grouped launches while preserving separate logical parameter matrices and MuonH update semantics.

Reuse [bench_grouped_wgrad.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grouped_wgrad.py) and [Hero diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py). Related work: #9077 (XLA/cuDNN ragged-dot replacement), #8311 (fused EP backend). Link existing results and avoid repeating covered comparisons without a new candidate or changed configuration.

Done when:

- Record pinned source/dependency versions, hardware, shapes, routing/group counts, warmup, timing boundary, repeated timings, and numerical comparisons for each candidate. Reuse identical seeded normal or checkpoint-derived operands across matched variants; include the operand seed or checkpoint in the recorded configuration.
- Separate kernel time, complete operator time, peak memory, and full training-step time. For any overlap candidate, compare an unsplit batch, sequential chunks, and chunks with communication overlapped against expert compute.
- Validate promising candidates in a bounded Hero-shaped run on the same hardware, checkpoint, batches, token-to-expert assignments after capacity filtering, precision, and optimizer as the control. Report forward/backward agreement, loss, dropped-assignment counts, memory, and throughput, including integration overhead.
- Publish a ranked adopt/defer/reject recommendation here, with commands and result/profile links. An outcome with no useful speedups is valid. Keep changes that alter the numerical recipe, including MXFP8, as separately evaluated follow-ups.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
Child of #6037.

## Description
The pooled fast-transformer quality scorer (#7040) emits a calibrated score in `[0,1]` and buckets it at fixed `0.2` cutpoints; a monotonic calibration anchors those cutpoints to the absolute oracle quality levels (1–5). Decide whether that is the right bucketization for building the training mix, vs quantiles or another scheme.

Requirement: buckets must be **coherent** — a bucket means a consistent quality level, comparable across heterogeneous sources — **and** large enough to be a usable unit to mix and consume in training.

Options and trade-offs:
- **Absolute threshold (current)**: bucket = absolute level, so a source's bucket mix reflects its true quality composition (math piles into q3/q4, safety into q1). But the tails are thin — on the 100B run q0 = 1.9%, q4 = 4.6% — so the extreme buckets may be too small to be usable mix units.
- **Quantiles**: each bucket is large by construction (equal mass), but relative-to-distribution. Per-source flattens every source to 20/20/20/20/20 and erases the quality signal; global drifts with corpus composition and drops the absolute-level anchor (loses cross-corpus comparability).
- **Other**: absolute cutpoints with merged/floored thin tails; a hybrid (absolute cutpoints plus a min-bucket-size floor); or fewer / asymmetric bands sized for the mix.

Bucketization lives in `experiments/datakit/cluster/quality/fast_transformer/score.py` (calibration remap + `np.digitize` on `BUCKET_EDGES`); calibration is fit in `calibrate.py`.

### Definition of Done
- Bucketization scheme chosen and documented with rationale, satisfying both properties: coherent / cross-source-comparable buckets **and** each bucket large enough to serve as a mix unit.
- Applied in `score.py` / `calibrate.py` and reflected in the July-hero mix construction.

issues.author: Calvin-Xu
issues.body:
## Summary

Audit whether nearby curriculum / specialized-pretraining papers rule out the possibility that a single-phase fixed-bucket mixture is optimal or near-optimal for our current data-mixing setting.

Current conclusion: they do not rule it out. The papers support the prior that phase/order effects can matter, but they do not imply that a two-phase schedule must substantially beat the best single-phase mixture for broad smooth objectives such as OLMoBaseEval Table-9 macro BPB or uncheatable BPB.

The key distinction is aggregate exposure versus phase placement. A clean phase-order test should hold aggregate exposure fixed,

$$
\bar w=\gamma_0 w^{(0)}+\gamma_1 w^{(1)},
$$

and vary only where buckets appear in training. Comparisons that change the amount of target-domain exposure cannot isolate the value of phase order.

## Papers Audited

### 1. Replaying pre-training data improves fine-tuning

**Setup in our terms.** This paper is closest to a two-bucket target-adaptation setup: generic data plus scarce target data. It studies target validation loss, using two-stage schedules parameterized by replay fraction \(\rho\) and target Stage-2 allocation \(\alpha\).

The paper's main schedule sweep is relevant because it explicitly varies phase placement. It finds that replay-only improves over a mid-training baseline, and the full schedule improves further for FineMath and Flan. StarCoder is a useful counterexample: replay-only and full schedule both report \(1.53\times\) data-efficiency improvement, so phase-placement gains are not universal even in their two-domain setting.

**Why the highlighted Appendix H.2 statement does not prove single-phase suboptimality.** Appendix H.2 fits a reference scaling law by changing how many target tokens the reference algorithm sees. The reference runs are uniform-throughout: the authors write that they "mix data uniformly throughout training." They then note that reference runs with "extra data outperform the best data orders" in the low-target-data setting.

That comparison changes aggregate target exposure. It says that a uniform-throughout reference algorithm with more target data can beat clever schedules that only receive the low target-data budget used in the main paper. That is evidence that aggregate exposure can dominate schedule effects, not evidence that single-phase mixtures are intrinsically suboptimal.

**Deviation from our current setting.**

- Their objective is target-domain validation loss, not a broad macro BPB objective.
- Their target data is scarce and repeated.
- Their schedule is low-dimensional and manually swept.
- Their data-efficiency metric is defined through a reference scaling law, not direct optimization of a fixed policy class.
- Learning-rate schedule and cooldown placement are part of the treatment.

The two-domain aspect is not itself a reason to discount the paper. We also have an internal StarCoder/Nemotron two-domain, two-phase landscape where the observed global optimum is near the single-phase diagonal. That makes the replay paper structurally relevant, but it also reinforces that phase asymmetry can be small for some objectives.

### 2. The Finetuner's Fallacy: When to Pretrain with Your Finetuning Data

**Setup in our terms.** This paper studies domain adaptation with a general corpus and one specialized domain dataset. The main comparison is:

- NPT: pretrain on general data, then finetune on domain data.
- SPT: mix a small fraction \(\delta\) of domain data throughout pretraining, then finetune on domain data.

In our notation, the pretraining part of SPT is close to a one-phase mixture,

$$
w_{\mathrm{domain}}=\delta,\qquad w_{\mathrm{general}}=1-\delta.
$$

The paper then appends a separate finetuning policy and evaluates post-finetuning domain test loss.

**Does it rule out single-phase near-optimality?** No. If anything, it supports the idea that diffuse early exposure can be strong. SPT has domain data present throughout pretraining as a small fraction of tokens. Its success argues against the opposite extreme: all general data first, then all domain data only during finetuning.

The paper does show that timing matters: early domain exposure is not fully replaced by replay-based later training in their MusicPile setting. It also finds that the best \(\delta\) depends on compute budget and dataset size. This supports a budget- and repetition-dependent view of phase effects, not a universal claim that late two-phase schedules dominate.

**Deviation from our current setting.**

- It includes finetuning after pretraining; our current scaling validations evaluate trained checkpoints directly.
- \(\delta\) controls both mixture composition and repetition of a small domain corpus.
- The objective is post-finetuning specialized-domain test loss, not broad macro BPB.
- The question is when domain data should enter before finetuning, not whether two learned pretraining phases beat one fixed pretraining mixture.

The one-domain setup remains relevant. Our StarCoder landscape is also effectively a two-domain phase-order test. The more important difference is the downstream protocol and objective, not the number of domains.

## What Contradicts Our Findings?

The papers contradict any strong claim that phase/order never matters. Both provide regimes where when data appears during training changes performance.

They do not directly contradict our current observation that single-phase candidates are competitive for broad smooth objectives. The replay paper itself has a StarCoder case where full phase scheduling does not improve beyond replay-only, and the Finetuner's Fallacy paper is partly evidence for the strength of diffuse early exposure.

The careful synthesis is:

- The two-phase policy class is larger in principle.
- Our current two-phase solver has not reliably harvested a transferable phase-asymmetry advantage.
- Prior work says such advantages can exist, but their magnitude depends on objective, exposure, repetition, scale, and downstream protocol.
- The decisive next test is a matched-exposure phase-order experiment.

## Proposed Next Experiment

Run a matched-exposure phase-order DOE:

1. Choose strong aggregate mixtures \(\bar w\), including the best single-phase mixtures.
2. Generate two-phase variants with the same \(\bar w\) but different phase placement.
3. Validate whether Table-9 macro BPB or uncheatable BPB changes beyond the 3e18 noise floor.

This directly tests whether phase placement itself matters in our regime, without confounding it with aggregate exposure.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Record the literature conclusion: these papers motivate phase-order tests but do not rule out single-phase near-optimality.
- [ ] Define the matched-exposure phase-order experiment.
- [ ] If we run follow-up experiments, report whether phase-placement changes are larger than the measured 3e18 noise floor.

issues.body:
**Agent-driven experiment issue** — this research loop, its logbook, and the updates posted here are maintained by a Claude agent (per `.agents/skills/run-research`), supervised by @mcwitt.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

The FP8 ragged-dot backward optimization loop improved the grug MoE H100 fwd+bwd acceptance speedups from w13 1.32x to 1.41x and w2 1.19x to 1.27x versus the tuned bf16 Triton baseline at the tpe=1024 operating point. The wins came from retuning Mosaic block configs for fwd/dgrad, setting wgrad grid_block_n=1, using a 64-row cast tile, and replacing wgrad's in-SMEM boundary mask with a pre-masked boundary appendix so the pipeline body is branch-free. GPU numerics pass on stock jaxlib, and a jaxlib 0.10.1 mixed FP8 fork validation later showed the intended e5m2 x e4m3 backward recipe matches uniform FP8 performance. The largest remaining non-kernel lever is hoisting weight quantization across grad-accumulation microbatches; measured caching would lift layer-level fwd+bwd throughput by about 15% at the canonical point.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6930#issuecomment-4880310767
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6930#issuecomment-4880353349
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6930#issuecomment-4882504309
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Research loop to speed up the FP8 ragged GEMM backward for the grug MoE layer on H100.

**Status quo at start:** ~1.32x forward / weak backward (~1.19x at w2) against a 2x arithmetic ceiling. dgrad reused the forward-tuned config; wgrad (`mgpu_dwgrad`) had a hardcoded 128-token tile, Lane-semantics lowering, and per-tile boundary masking.

**Logbook:** `.agents/logbooks/fp8-gemm-speed.md` on branch `research/fp8-gemm-speed` (raw results in `lib/haliax/bench/results/`). Prior art: GFP8-OPT loop in `.agents/logbooks/grug-fp8-ragged.md` on `grug-fp8-fork`.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Loop update (FPB-P02..P05): the canonical-point fwd+bwd speedup moved **1.297x → 1.382x (w13)** and **1.21x → 1.27x (w2)** from three pure config changes (no kernel edits, numerics untouched):

- `_autotuned_config` (fwd + dgrad): (192,128,128,mcs5) → (128,128,128,mcs6) — the old 192 tuning was an artifact of the coupled fwd+dgrad autotune; the shorter accumulator halves register pressure and buys a deeper pipeline (~10-14% per GEMM).
- `_dwgrad_config`: grid_block_n 2 → 1 (~6-8% on the wgrad).

Falsified along the way: i8 bitwise mask (cost is the SMEM round-trip, not converts), SM oversubscription (SMEM budget halving beats overlap gains), ladder zero-stores (Mosaic swizzle forbids sub-tile SMEM column stores), Warpgroup-semantics port (layout inference fails).

In flight: **boundary appendix** — structural elimination of the wgrad's in-SMEM boundary masking (pre-masked first/last token blocks written next to the operand by the cast; the pipeline index_map redirects there; body becomes branch-free). issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
**Agent-driven experiment issue** — this research loop, its logbook, and the updates posted here are maintained by a Claude agent (per `.agents/skills/run-research`), supervised by @mcwitt.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This FP8 grug MoE layer spike met its >=1.4x end-to-end target on 2-node H100 EP16: the final ring-backend measurement was bf16 33.47 ms/step versus FP8 23.28 ms/step, or 1.438x. The investigation found that FP8 should be used on permutation legs only: dispatch all_gather forward carries e4m3, combine-transpose all_gather backward carries e5m2, and reductions remain native bf16 because decomposing ring psum_scatter into FP8 all_to_all plus local sum regressed cross-node performance. Deliverables were pushed as two opt-in branches, `fp8-moe-mlp` for FP8 expert GEMM wiring and `fp8-moe-mlp-comms` for FP8 wire traffic. Defaults remain bf16 until scientific validation, because the full-layer FP8 mechanism is only performance-derisked so far.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6911#issuecomment-4878544634
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6911#issuecomment-4878649652
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

Research spike to derisk FP8 comms/collectives in the grug MoE layer.

**Goal:** grug MoE MLP layer running end-to-end in FP8 — all expert GEMMs *and* the
dispatch/combine (permute/unpermute) collectives carrying FP8 over the wire — demonstrating
**≥ 1.4× fwd+bwd speedup vs the existing bf16 configuration** at realistic operating parameters
(D=2560, I=1280, E=256, K=4, L=26, B=8192·x; EP4 on H100).

**Deliverables (post-spike):** two review-optimized branches:
1. `fp8-moe-mlp` (based on `fp8-ragged-dot-mixed-fork`): wiring to enable FP8 in the MoE MLP GEMMs
   (`Fp8RaggedDotOp` through the EP backends, delayed-scaling state under shard_map).
2. `fp8-moe-mlp-comms` (based on `fp8-moe-mlp`): dispatch/combine collectives in FP8 over the wire
   (e4m3 forward activations / e5m2 backward gradients), where the speedup beyond the GEMM-only
   1.29× comes from.

**Approach:** adapt the default "ring" backend first (all_gather dispatch → e4m3; psum_scatter
combine decomposed into fp8 all_to_all + local bf16 sum); fall back to the `ragged_all_to_all`
backend (both legs are already wire permutations) if ring proves infeasible.

**Logbook:** `.agents/logbooks/fp8-moe-comms.md` on branch `research/fp8-moe-comms`
(ID prefix `FP8MOE`). Baseline GEMM-level results: haliax `fp8-ragged-dot` PR family
(per-GEMM 1.31×/1.19×; expert-MLP layer 1.29× at the operating point).

FP8 remains **off by default** — this spike derisks mechanism + performance; scientific
validation before any training run is explicitly out of scope.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Spike result: goal met — 1.43× end-to-end at 2-node EP16 on the default ring backend.**

Full e2e MoE layer (fwd+bwd, routing dispatch + EP collectives + expert GEMMs + combine) at the
operating parameters (D=2560, I=1280, E=256, K=4, T_local=16384/device, non-uniform routing),
throughput timer, H100s on `cw-us-east-02a`:

| scale | layout | bf16 ms | fp8 GEMMs | + FP8 wire | best speedup |
|-------|--------|---------|-----------|------------|--------------|
| 1 node (8×H100, NVLink) | EP4×data2 | 23.44 | 20.33 | 19.81 | 1.18× |
| **2 nodes (16×H100, IB)** | **EP16** | **33.80** | 27.52 | **23.63** | **1.43×** |
| 2 nodes | EP8-intra×data2 | 37.28 | 33.98 | 31.60 | 1.18× |
| 2 nodes (a2a backend) | EP16 | 35.87 | 29.57 | 24.19 | 1.48× vs a2a bf16 |

Key findings:
- **FP8 belongs on permutation legs only.** Decomposing the ring `psum_scatter` combine into an
  FP8 all_to_all + local sum *regressed* 0.885× cross-node: NCCL's hierarchical reduce-scatter
  reduces node-locally before crossing IB, which byte-halving cannot repay. Final design: dispatch
  all_gather fwd = E4M3, combine-transpose all_gather bwd = E5M2, reductions native bf16.
- Intra-node (NVLink), collectives are fully hidden under pipelined compute — FP8 wire is ~free
  but not needed; the single-node win is the FP8 GEMMs (1.15–1.22×).
- The EP8-intra-node layout (MoE comms on NVLink only) is *slower* in bf16 than EP16 — DP
  weight-grad allreduce over IB dominates — so 1.43× is against the strongest bf16 config.
- `ragged_all_to_all` backend: 4× slower than ring intra-node (local permute machinery), near
  parity cross-node; its FP8 wire (`fp8_ragged_a2a` with an efficient custom transpose) gives the
  largest same-backend gain (1.48×).
- Numerics through the full FP8 layer: fwd out relfrob ~4e-2, dx ~1.0–1.2e-1. Mechanism is
  derisked; **scientific validation is still required before any training run — default stays bf16.**

Next: organizing into two review-optimized branches — `fp8-moe-mlp` (FP8 MoE MLP GEMM wiring, on
`fp8-ragged-dot-mixed-fork`) and `fp8-moe-mlp-comms` (FP8 over-the-wire dispatch/combine, on
`fp8-moe-mlp`). Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/fp8-moe-comms.md` on `research/fp8-moe-comms`.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Deliverable branches pushed** (spike sealed; logbook `FP8MOE-006`):

- **`fp8-moe-mlp`** (based on `fp8-ragged-dot-mixed-fork`): FP8 wiring for the MoE MLP GEMMs — `MoeRaggedDotOps` (per-GEMM `Fp8RaggedDotOp` state, like two `Linear`s' `Fp8DotGeneralOp`s) threaded through `moe_mlp` / `MoEExpertMlp` into the EP ring + ragged_all_to_all backends, with a pmax-cotangent wrapper so delayed-scaling amax state combines as a max across shards rather than shard_map's psum.
- **`fp8-moe-mlp-comms`** (based on `fp8-moe-mlp`): FP8 over-the-wire dispatch/combine — `fp8_wire` module (E4M3 fwd / E5M2 bwd, per-sender current scaling, **permutation legs only**; reductions stay native bf16) + the `fp8_wire` flag through both EP backends.

Validation of the final branch code: 10/10 tests on 8×H100 (CPU-runnable except the ragged-a2a parity test), and a cross-node spot check reproducing the headline: ring EP16 bf16 33.47 → fp8 23.28 ms/step = **1.438×** on 2×8×H100 over IB.

Everything is opt-in; **defaults stay bf16** pending scientific validation (relfrob(dx) ≈ 1e-1 through the full FP8 layer). Bench harness + full measurement record: `research/fp8-moe-comms`.

comments.author: dlwh-golem
comments.body: @dlwh Added a managed experiment TL;DR block summarizing the final 1.438x EP16 result, FP8-wire recommendation, deliverable branches, and supporting result comments; applied the `tldr` label.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Post-seal follow-ups (2026-07-03/04): fused e4m3 dispatch, EP32 scale results, a2a backend fix.** Logbook: [`fp8-moe-h3h4.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/fp8-moe-h3h4/.agents/logbooks/fp8-moe-h3h4.md) on `research/fp8-moe-h3h4` (entries H3H4-001…006). Same operating parameters as the spike (D=2560/I=1280/E=256/K=4, T_local=16384/device).

- **Fused e4m3 dispatch (H3+H4 from the spike's follow-up queue)**: quantize once with the w13 op's delayed replicated scale → byte all_gather → byte capacity-take → straight into the FP8 GEMM under one custom_vjp; reductions stay bf16. Needed a tiled Triton byte transpose in the backward (XLA's uncoalesced 1-byte transpose, 2.9 ms/step, ate the entire win). Results: EP4 **1.203×** (vs fp8wire 1.188×), EP32 ring **1.467×** (vs 1.375×) — the gain scales with the gathered buffer, as designed. relfrob(dx) unchanged at 1.05e-1; relfrob(loss) slightly better (one fewer quantization). `H3H4-002`/`003`.
- **EP32 (4 nodes, 32×H100) backend crossover**: ring's dispatch volume grows ~linearly with EP size and falls off the cliff (bf16 33.8→53.7 ms/step from EP16→EP32 at constant per-device work); the a2a backend caps near top-k. Best-vs-best: **a2a+fp8wire 26.60 ms/step = 1.76× its own bf16, 2.02× vs the ring-bf16 production point** (+38% over ring's best, fp8fused at 36.64). a2a is the scale backend; porting the fused dispatch to its dispatch leg is the queued next step. `H3H4-005`.
- **a2a intra-node deficit root-caused** (corrects the spike-era "local permute machinery" hypothesis): XLA's one-shot single-host ragged-a2a kernel runs at ~12 GB/s effective; `--xla_gpu_unsupported_use_ragged_all_to_all_one_shot_kernel=false` routes it through NCCL — **96.3 → 26.5 ms/step** at EP4-intra-node, within 14% of ring. Multi-host is unaffected (never uses that kernel). jax 0.10's builtin ragged-a2a AD transpose is already efficient (a hand-written custom_vjp changed nothing). Docs + runtime-warning branch `grug-moe-a2a-oneshot-flag` is pushed; PR deferred. `H3H4-006`.

Baseline note: these runs predate the GEMM-stack retune in #6930 (per-GEMM now w13 1.41× / w2 1.27×), so the FP8 columns above are, if anything, conservative.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Two pieces were deliberately deferred out of PR3 (#6835, handoff + FederationSync) to keep it focused. Both are safe to add later without changing the handoff/sync wire protocol.

## 1. Cross-cluster spend caps for federated roots

A handed-off (federated) root has zero local tasks, so it does not count toward local spend, and there is no aggregate view of what a user is spending across peers. A user can therefore exceed their intended cap by fanning work out to peers.

PR3 removed the earlier per-handle `spend_snapshot_micros` budget check (local spend + cached federated spend + this job's reservation vs the user cap): it was a single-cluster approximation bolted onto a per-handoff row and did not compose across more than one peer. The column was written-only after the check was dropped, so it was removed rather than left dormant.

A real solution needs:

- A **cross-cluster spend model**: a user's total = local spend + the live spend of every job they have federated to every peer, refreshed as `FederationSync` mirrors peer task state back. The mirrored task rows already carry enough state to value a federated job the same way a local one is valued.
- Admission at handoff time that consults that aggregate, not a per-row snapshot — so N concurrent handoffs to N peers can't each individually pass a cap they jointly exceed.
- A decision on **where** the cap lives: the requesting (parent) controller at submit/handoff, the peer at receive, or both. The parent is the only place that sees a user's whole cross-cluster footprint.
- Interaction with the existing `UserBudgetDefaults` / local budget-admission path, so a user has one cap, not one-per-cluster.

## 2. `federation_changelog` retention / pruning

The peer-side `federation_changelog` is append-only — one row per received-job/task mutation, no FK to `jobs` (so a tombstone survives the job delete). PR3 lands no pruner, so on a busy peer it grows without bound.

Pruning is safe to add without touching the sync protocol: a row can be dropped once every configured requester's cursor has advanced past its `seq` (a min-cursor floor). The `FederationSync` staleness path already handles a requester whose cursor has fallen below the retained window — it drives a full-resync set-replacement, exactly as first contact does — so pruning never loses correctness, only history.

Open question: whether the floor is computed from persisted per-requester cursors on the peer, or requesters advertise their low-water mark on each sync.

## 3. Write-lock contention from large sync batches

The federation sync loop runs on its own thread and makes its blocking `FederationSync` RPC to the peer *outside* any write transaction, so the controller's write lock is never held across network I/O. But it then applies the batch in one `apply_sync_batch()` transaction, which does hold the write lock for the duration of the mirror/delete writes. For an incremental batch that's a handful of rows, but a first-contact **full resync** returns the requester's entire active set, so a large mirror (plus any tombstone `delete_job` cascades) can hold the write lock long enough to briefly stall the control tick's end-of-tick commit.

This is the same class of contention as `prune_old_data`'s bulk-delete transaction and is bounded per-peer, so PR3 leaves it as-is. If it shows up in practice, options are: chunk `apply_sync_batch()` into several smaller write transactions, or cap the number of deltas per sync response and let the cursor advance across rounds. Surfaced by a peer-review pass on PR #6835.

Part of #6718.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — design follow-up, not opening a PR.**

Both items are new subsystems with open design decisions, and they build directly on machinery that only exists in **PR #6835** (`weaver/iris-federation-pr3-handoff-sync`), which is still open. The `federation_changelog` table and the handoff/`FederationSync` loop these items extend are not on `main` yet, so implementing now would fork against an unmerged branch. Posting root cause + approach for review; sequence after #6835 lands.

# Research

On `main`, migration `0034_federation` already adds the federation sidecars, but the changelog table and sync/handoff manager are introduced by #6835.

**Relevant code (main @ `cf9756a`)**
- [`schema.py#L584`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/schema.py#L584) — `federated_jobs.spend_snapshot_micros` (per-handle federated spend)
- [`schema.py#L591-L598`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/schema.py#L591-L598) — `federation_sync_state`: per-peer opaque changelog `cursor`
- [`schema.py#L419`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/schema.py#L419) — `local_tasks` fold-exclusion: federated rows (`child_cluster != ''`) never count toward spend
- [`budget.py#L43-L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/budget.py#L43-L90) — `compute_user_spend` (local-only) + `compute_effective_band` cap gate
- [`pruner.py#L52-L70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/pruner.py#L52-L70) — one-delete-per-tx incremental prune loop (pattern to reuse)

# Proposed approach

## 1. Cross-cluster spend caps

Root cause: `compute_user_spend` sums only `local_tasks`; federated jobs are folded out at [`schema.py#L419`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/schema.py#L419), so a user's spend on peers is invisible and the per-handle `spend_snapshot_micros` snapshot doesn't compose across >1 peer.

- **Where the cap lives → the parent (requesting) controller**, at submit/handoff admission. It is the only node that sees a user's whole cross-cluster footprint; a peer sees only what was handed to it. Keep one cap per user via the existing `UserBudgetDefaults` / `compute_effective_band` path — don't add a per-cluster cap.
- **Aggregate model**: `user_total = compute_user_spend(local) + Σ live spend of that user's federated jobs`. Value each mirrored federated job with the *same* `resource_value` used locally, sourced from the peer task rows `FederationSync` already mirrors back — not from the frozen `spend_snapshot_micros` snapshot. That makes the snapshot column's removal (noted in the issue) moot: value from live mirrored state instead.
- **Admission**: evaluate the aggregate at handoff time so N concurrent handoffs to N peers can't each individually pass a cap they jointly exceed (serialize the check under the submit tx, as local admission already is).

Depends on #6835 mirroring peer task state with enough fidelity to re-run `resource_value`; confirm before implementing.

## 2. `federation_changelog` retention

Append-only, no FK to `jobs` (tombstones outlive job deletes), no pruner in #6835 → unbounded growth on a busy peer.

- **Min-cursor floor**: drop a changelog row once every requester's persisted cursor has advanced past its `seq`. Reuse the incremental one-delete-per-tx loop shape from [`pruner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9756a84c0a48845137b848cada82d39516822c/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/pruner.py#L52-L70) so pruning interleaves with sync traffic.
- **Open question → compute the floor from persisted per-requester cursors on the peer**, not from a low-water mark requesters advertise. The peer already persists per-peer cursors (`federation_sync_state`), so the floor is a local `MIN(cursor)` with no wire-protocol change. Advertising a low-water mark would add a field and a round-trip for no correctness gain.
- **Safety**: a requester whose cursor falls below the retained window is already handled by the `FederationSync` staleness path (full-resync set-replacement), so pruning loses history, never correctness.

Sequence after #6835 to avoid conflicting with the changelog schema/writer it introduces.

Part of #6718.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 A federation architecture review turned up concrete evidence for both items here — recording it so whoever picks this up has the exact pointers.

**Changelog retention.** The stale-cursor machinery presupposes a compaction floor that was never written: `changelog_min_seq` (`reads.py`) and the `stale = cursor_seq < min_seq - 1` check (`service.py` federation_sync) assume rows below a floor get deleted, but nothing deletes `federation_changelog` rows — they're appended on every mutation of a received job (`writes.py`) and never pruned. So `min_seq` stays 1 forever and `cursor_stale` can only ever fire on first contact. The `writes.py` section header literally promises "changelog retention". Net: unbounded table growth on any busy peer, and the full-resync fallback is effectively unreachable in steady state. A pruner that keeps the latest seq per job and deletes below a floor fixes both.

**Spend cap bypass.** The plumbing is a three-layer stub: `PeerSummary.aggregate_spend_micros` (proto) is never populated (`manager.py` `_build_summary`), the `aggregateSpendMicros` TS mirror is never rendered, and the backing `spend_snapshot_micros` column — created in migration 0034 — was silently dropped by the 0035 rebuild (absent from both the CREATE and the copy SELECT). Meanwhile a federated handle has zero local task rows, so the task-count-based submit cap and scheduler spend never see it. A user can exceed their cap by fanning work to peers, exactly as described above.

(Surfaced alongside #6912 / #6913 / #6914 from the same review; the dead `aggregate_spend_micros` field is noted in #6913's drop-or-wire list, deferring the decision to this issue's budget work.)

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
We currently capture CPU, RAM & thread stack profiles for all Iris jobs. This allows us to to useful post-mortem & aggregate optimization across all jobs we're running.

Let's additionally sample accelerator profiles and write them to WandB/Finelog. This should be combined with an analysis agent from #6464 which would investigate jobs running for the day and identify potential causes of slowdown.

For the benefit of said profiling agent, we should additionally track the git repo/branch/upstream information when jobs are submitted: this would let the agent examine (public) repository code and suggest performance improvements for users.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue + check #6464 and open PRs/issues for duplicates
- [x] Survey existing Iris profiling + job-submission infrastructure
- [x] Post Research + Proposed approach (design-level; no PR)

Scope is a new feature spanning the proto schema, the worker profiling loop, and job-submission provenance — well over 100 lines and multi-module. Posting analysis for human review instead of opening a PR. No duplicate PRs/issues found.

# Research

Two requests: (1) periodic **accelerator** (xprof) profiling alongside the existing CPU/RAM/thread sampling, written to the same sink; (2) capture submitter **git repo/branch/upstream** at submission so the #6464 analysis agent can read public source.

Existing profiling is host-only. The worker periodic loop captures a CPU speedscope per running attempt via `py-spy` (external ptrace attach) and writes one `IrisProfile` row to finelog namespace `iris.profile`. There is **no** accelerator path: `grep -r 'xprof|xplane|jax.profiler' lib/iris` is empty. JAX tracing exists only inside training (`jax.profiler.start_trace`), and **no** `jax.profiler.start_server` runs in any job — so xprof cannot be sampled by external attach the way py-spy is; capture must be triggered in the JAX process.

The only git info tracked today is `IRIS_GIT_HASH`, the *image build* commit baked at build time — not the submitter working tree, branch, or remote URL.

**Relevant code**
- [`worker.py#L1027-L1062`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L1027-L1062) — periodic loop, CPU-only, `ProfileTrigger.PERIODIC`
- [`profile.py#L43-L106`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/profile.py#L43-L106) — `ProfileType`/`IrisProfile`/format maps; py-spy + memray subprocess model
- [`job.proto#L86-L139`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L86-L139) — `CpuProfile`/`MemoryProfile`/`ThreadsProfile`, `ProfileType` oneof
- [`remote_client.py#L123-L191`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/remote_client.py#L123-L191) — `submit_job`; sends `client_revision_date`, no git provenance
- [`job.proto#L150-L161`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L150-L161) — `ProcessInfo.git_hash` (build-time only)

# Proposed Approach (design change — needs review before implementation)

**Part B (git provenance) is the small, low-risk half and should land first.**

Capture submitter git state in `RemoteClusterClient.submit_job` (`git rev-parse HEAD`, `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`, `config --get remote.origin.url`, `status --porcelain` for a dirty flag), each best-effort/`None` outside a repo. Add a `GitProvenance` message (`commit`, `branch`, `remote_url`, `dirty`) to the `LaunchJobRequest`, persist it on the job record, and surface it in job status so the #6464 agent can map a slow job to public source. ~80–150 LOC; testable end-to-end via a temp-repo submission asserting the recorded fields. Distinct enough to be its own PR.

**Part A (accelerator profiling) is the larger design question.** External attach does not work for xprof. Two viable models:

1. **In-process JAX profiler server + remote capture.** Jobs call `jax.profiler.start_server(port)` at startup; the worker periodic loop triggers a timed capture against that port (xprof/TF profiler client), collecting the `xplane.pb`. Pros: matches the existing "worker samples the task periodically" shape, no training-loop edits per job. Cons: every accelerator job must start the server and expose the port; capture client is a new dependency; only JAX jobs participate.
2. **In-process triggered trace.** A signal/sentinel-file hook wraps `start_trace`/`stop_trace` inside the run; the worker requests a window, the job writes the trace to a known path, the worker uploads it. Pros: reuses Levanter's existing tracing. Cons: requires opt-in instrumentation in each job's loop; weaker for arbitrary jobs.

I lean toward **(1)**: it generalizes to any JAX process and keeps the worker as the scheduler, consistent with the CPU path. Either way:

- Extend the proto `ProfileType` oneof with an `AcceleratorProfile` (xplane/Perfetto format) and add `accelerator`/`xplane` to `ProfileType`/`ProfileFormat`/format maps in `profile.py`.
- Store the trace as an `IrisProfile` row (`type=accelerator`, `trigger=periodic`) in `iris.profile` — same sink as CPU, so existing finelog→WandB plumbing and `job_profile_summary.py` extend naturally rather than adding a parallel store.
- Periodic accelerator capture should be opt-in per job (heavier than py-spy) and skipped on workers with no accelerator.

**Open questions for a human:**
- Capture mechanism (1) vs (2)?
- WandB *and* finelog, or finelog-only with the WandB view derived downstream?
- Default cadence/duration for accelerator captures, and opt-in vs on-by-default for TPU/GPU jobs?

Suggest splitting into two PRs: git provenance first (mergeable now), accelerator profiling after the capture-mechanism decision.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The goal of this thread is to conduct a reasonably comprehensive feature comparison between popular RL frameworks using AI agents to quickly explore the state of the codebases.

We will not establish in this guide the degree to which the frameworks are *actually capable* of doing what they report being able to do; that will be a later issue.

End-goal is a reasonably constrained search space of candidate frameworks.

STARTING POINT

Frameworks: veRL, slime, miles, SkyRL, OpenRLHF, ROLL, AReaL, prime-rl, NeMO-RL, [torchforge](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/torchforge) + [monarch](https://github.com/meta-pytorch/monarch) (used by [Together.AI](http://together.ai/), monarch replaces Ray)

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
## MoE RL + Router Replay — feature comparison (agent-driven pass)

Ran the AI-agent codebase exploration this thread calls for: cloned all 10 frameworks and read source to compare **feature presence** for one concrete target — RL-training a large **hybrid-MoE** model (**Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B**: GatedDeltaNet linear-attention + 512-expert MoE) with **router replay** ([R3, arXiv:2510.11370](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370)) in an **agentic** RLVR setup. Per the thread's scope this is *what's wired*, not validated capability.

**Detailed per-framework reports (file:line evidence):** https://gist.github.com/penfever/83e3d070625b4de63fe93509dafb8fcd

### Decisive-axes table

| Framework (HEAD) | Router replay (R3) | Routed-experts capture | External agent → **vLLM**? | MoE backend + EP | Qwen3-Next |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **prime-rl** (`63af823`) | ✅ native, generic, **FSDP2**, **CI'd on the `qwen3_5` hybrid arch** | **stock vLLM** (`enable_return_routed_experts`, fork-free) | ❌ rollout = `verifiers` env | torchtitan FSDP2 + EP/DeepEP | ✅ `qwen3_5_moe` (the hybrid); 35B-A3B example |
| **veRL** (`d5fc06d`) | ✅ R2 + R3 (Megatron **and FSDP2/VeOmni**) | vLLM + SGLang (patched/fork) | ⚠️ pluggable `AgentLoopManager`; trainer still spins up own inference | Megatron + FSDP2 + EP | ✅ FSDP2 trainable; replay not wired for QN |
| **SLIME** (`44d29ee`) | ✅ CI-gated R3 (Megatron, patched mcore) | **SGLang** HTTP (`meta_info`) | ❌ SGLang-native | Megatron + EP | ✅ recipe; replay not CI'd w/ QN |
| **miles** (`c8b6697`, slime fork) | ✅ **the upstream R3**; controller generic/write-once | **SGLang-only** (forked `sglang-miles`) | ❌ no vLLM path | Megatron + EP (FSDP backend has no replay) | ✅ recipe; replay not CI'd w/ QN |
| **SkyRL** (`penfever/working`) | ⚠️ on `main` (Megatron-only), not on launch branch | **vLLM HTTP** (our fork emits over `/v1`) | ✅ already integrated (agentic + on-policy capture) | FSDP2 / Megatron | ⚠️ config + GatedDeltaNet kernels ready |
| **ROLL** (`51c123f`) | ❌ (off-by-default TIS substitute) | none from rollout | ⚠️ both engines, no capture | Megatron + EP | ✅ turnkey Megatron RLVR config |
| **NeMo-RL** (`49c9f16`) | ❌ (GSPO/IS substitute) | vLLM/SGLang, no capture | ❌ binds its own vLLM | Megatron + DTensor/FSDP2 + EP | 🔜 roadmap (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B nearest) |
| **AReaL** (`5e776c8`) | ❌ replay (**capture-only scaffold**) | SGLang (vLLM rejected) | ✅✅ OpenAI-proxy gateway hosts an external agent unmodified | Megatron / Archon-FSDP2 + EP/PP | ✅ strong hybrid impl (`archon/qwen3_5`) |
| **OpenRLHF** (`6c6056d`) | ❌ (TIS/GSPO/ICEPOP — probability-space only) | none (in-process vLLM) | ❌ in-process, no EP | DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 only, **no EP** | ⚠️ unproven |
| **torchforge + monarch** (`b32f06b`/`86f706b`) | ❌ | none (in-process vLLM) | ⚠️ paused v0.1.0 | torchtitan FSDP2 + EP | ❌ |

### Key findings
1. **Router replay exists in 4 of 10** — prime-rl, veRL, SLIME, miles (miles is the upstream R3; veRL/prime-rl track the same line). The rest substitute *probability-space* importance sampling (TIS/GSPO/ICEPOP), which corrects likelihood drift but **not** the expert-selection mismatch R3 targets.
2. **Replay is generic / write-once, not per-model.** Implementations patch a generic router (Megatron `TopKRouter` or a generic FSDP2 MoE-router hook); the only per-model surface is the HF↔backend converter you already need to serve the model. prime-rl's `test_qwen3_5_moe_router_replay` exercises replay on the GatedDeltaNet-hybrid MoE class.
3. **Capture is engine-bound** (vLLM *or* SGLang) and usually needs an inference-engine fork to emit `routed_experts`; the RL framework just sets a flag. prime-rl reports stock-vLLM 0.22 capture.
4. **The full combination (hybrid-MoE + R3 + agentic + a specific HTTP engine) is a drop-in nowhere** — every framework misses ≥1 axis for a given constraint set.

### Constrained candidate set
- **Genuine MoE router replay:** **prime-rl, veRL, SLIME, miles.** (OpenRLHF / NeMo-RL / AReaL / ROLL / torchforge have none today — AReaL has capture-only scaffolding; NeMo-RL is Megatron-strong but replay-less.)
- **Best reference implementation:** **prime-rl** — FSDP2-native, generic, hybrid-arch CI'd, fork-free stock-vLLM capture. **miles** (generic replay controller + merge/truncation-safe routed-experts rail) and **veRL** (`VeOmniRouterReplay`, FSDP2) are strong secondary references.
- **Strongest adopt-as-framework option:** **veRL** (only one combining R3 + an FSDP2 backend + a pluggable external-rollout seam).
- **AReaL** is worth noting for its OpenAI-proxy gateway (hosts any external agent unmodified) and a strong `archon/qwen3_5` hybrid impl — but no replay yet.

### Open (for the "actual capability" follow-up issue)
Router replay on Qwen3-Next-**80B** specifically is a shipped-example gap in *every* framework: the arch *class* is proven (prime-rl on `qwen3_5_moe`), the 80B size + each stack's integration are not.

*Sources:* repos/HEADs above; R3 [arXiv:2510.11370](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370); [miles](https://github.com/radixark/miles) ([LMSYS blog](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2025-11-19-miles/)). Full per-framework reports with file:line citations in the [gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/83e3d070625b4de63fe93509dafb8fcd).

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
## Recommendation & reasoning

Following the feature comparison above, here's my recommendation for the constrained search space. (Still feature-reasoning, not validated capability — that's the follow-up issue.)

### What the decision hinges on
For our target — agentic RLVR on a **hybrid-MoE** model (Qwen3-Next-class: GatedDeltaNet + 512-expert MoE) — four features matter, and they interact:
1. **Router replay (R3)** — without it, MoE GRPO risks train↔inference router-mismatch collapse ([arXiv:2510.11370](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370)); probability-space correction (TIS/GSPO) doesn't address it.
2. **Agentic, multi-turn rollout** with tool/sandbox + verifier reward.
3. **Keep the existing agentic harness ([Harbor](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor)) driving an HTTP-served vLLM** as the rollout layer (hard constraint for us).
4. **MoE training with expert parallelism** (FSDP2-or-Megatron + EP).

No single framework ships all four as a drop-in (see table), so the real question is *build vs adopt*, and the deciding axis is #3 (the engine/harness coupling).

### Recommendation
**Primary — build it into SkyRL, keep Harbor→vLLM.** Implement router replay as a capture→training rail + a generic FSDP2 replay hook in our SkyRL/Harbor/vLLM stack. Rationale:
- It's the **only** stack where the agentic + HTTP-vLLM rollout and on-policy token-fidelity capture are **already integrated**, and our vLLM fork **already emits `routed_experts` over `/v1`** — so we keep Harbor with no migration.
- **Replay is generic / write-once** (every framework patches a generic router, not per-model), so this is a bounded one-time build that serves future MoE models too.
- Strong reference implementations exist to port from: **prime-rl** (FSDP2-native, generic, CI'd on the `qwen3_5` hybrid arch — the closest match), with **miles** (generic replay controller + merge/truncation-safe routed-experts rail) and **veRL** (`VeOmniRouterReplay`, FSDP2) secondary.

**Alternative — adopt veRL.** If we'd rather not build in-house, veRL is the strongest adopt-as-framework option: the only one combining R3 + an **FSDP2** backend + a **pluggable external-rollout seam** (`AgentLoopManager` is "designed to be fully replaceable"), so Harbor could drive it. Costs: the trainer still spins up its own (idle) inference replicas, we'd re-implement token-fidelity in its `DataProto` format, and the Agent-Loop API is alpha.

**Why not the others:**
- **SLIME / miles** — genuine R3, but **SGLang-only**; conflicts with the keep-vLLM constraint (miles is the reference R3 impl, so it's a code reference, not an adopt target for us).
- **ROLL / NeMo-RL / OpenRLHF / torchforge** — no router replay (NeMo-RL is Megatron+EP-strong but replay-less; OpenRLHF is DeepSpeed-only with no EP; torchforge is paused).
- **AReaL** — best external-rollout seam (OpenAI-proxy gateway hosts an external agent unmodified) and a strong hybrid arch impl, but replay is **capture-only scaffolding** (no replay loss) and it rejects vLLM capture. Worth tracking; its gateway is a reference design if we ever decouple Harbor from a trainer.

### Deferred to the capability-validation issue
Router replay on Qwen3-Next-**80B** specifically is a shipped-example gap **everywhere** — the arch *class* is proven (prime-rl CI's replay on `qwen3_5_moe`), but the 80B size and each stack's end-to-end integration are not. Validation items: capture↔layer alignment on the hybrid stack, shared-expert exclusion from the routed mask, duplicate-index under EP/all-to-all, and FSDP2 backward through GatedDeltaNet+MoE under offload.

*(Comparison table + per-framework reports: the comment above + [gist](https://gist.github.com/penfever/83e3d070625b4de63fe93509dafb8fcd).)*

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
> Keep the existing agentic harness ([Harbor](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor?rgh-link-date=2026-06-04T13%3A29%3A31.000Z)) driving an HTTP-served vLLM as the rollout layer (hard constraint for us).

Does Harbor / Terminus 2 / LiteLLM require vLLM or works with any OpenAI http API provider?

It seems likely that we'll have to maintain a thin fork of vLLM to support our custom model and give us some extra freedom. Building on top of sglang is likely to be more work than using vLLM, but it's not entirely clear to me _how much_ more work. 

FWIW, I'd personally prefer us to use vLLM over sglang, as we paved this path a little more, but I don't think we should rule out sglang based RL frameworks only on the basis that they don't use vLLM.

For my own knowledge: besides (1) vLLM being more established than sglang and (2) we already somewhat use vLLM, what are the other reasons why we'd prefer using vLLM over sglang?

issues.author: wmoss
issues.body:
Currently to set Zephyr to run with the `InlineRunner` requires passing it in to `ZephyrContext`. The `ZephyrContext` is usually created in shared code (e.g. `lib/marin/src/marin/processing/classification/deduplication/exact.py`). It would be nice to be able to set this per-run.

Options I can think of off the cuff,
1. Command line parameter (plumbed through to `ZephyrContext`)
2. Environment variable (but I sort of hate these)

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue, AGENTS.md, fix-issue/pull-request skills
- [x] Locate `ZephyrContext` definition and all call sites
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PRs/issues)
- [x] Post research + proposed approach
- [ ] Await human direction on which option to take before implementing

# Research

`ZephyrContext.stage_runner_factory` is the only knob to swap `InlineRunner` ↔ `SubprocessRunner`. The default is picked by `_default_stage_runner_factory_for(client)` in `__post_init__`: `LocalClient` → `InlineRunner`, distributed → `SubprocessRunner`. There are ~30 production call sites that construct `ZephyrContext(...)` (deduplication, tokenize, datakit/download, classification), so changing the runner today means editing whichever shared module owns the construction.

**Relevant code**
- [\`execution.py#L1658-L1739\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1658-L1739) — \`ZephyrContext\` + \`__post_init__\`
- [\`execution.py#L329-L348\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L329-L348) — default factory selection
- [\`execution.py#L1718-L1726\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1718-L1726) — existing \`ZEPHYR_MAX_WORKERS\` env precedent
- [\`runners.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/runners.py) — \`InlineRunner\` / \`SubprocessRunner\`
- [\`exact.py#L78-L85\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/processing/classification/deduplication/exact.py#L78-L85) — representative shared-code construction

# Proposed Fix

Two viable options; both keep an explicit \`stage_runner_factory=...\` kwarg as the highest-priority override.

**Option A — env var \`ZEPHYR_STAGE_RUNNER=inline|subprocess\`** (~30 lines, self-contained in \`execution.py\` + a test). Reads in \`__post_init__\` only when \`stage_runner_factory is None\`. Mirrors the existing \`ZEPHYR_MAX_WORKERS\` pattern, requires zero call-site changes, lets \`ZEPHYR_STAGE_RUNNER=inline uv run ...\` flip the runner per-invocation. Downsides: AGENTS.md flags env-vars-over-explicit-params as a pitfall, and the issue notes \"I sort of hate these.\"

**Option B — command-line / config plumbing.** Add \`stage_runner: Literal[\"inline\", \"subprocess\"] | None\` to each shared entry point (\`dedup_exact_*\`, \`fuzzy_*\`, \`tokenize\`, datakit downloaders, etc.) and forward into \`ZephyrContext\`. ~30 callsites to update plus the public CLI configs that wrap them. Cleaner per AGENTS.md, but a multi-module change well over the 100-line bar — needs a design pass on which entry points actually need it and what the parameter name should be.

I lean toward Option A as the minimally-disruptive fix: it solves the stated pain (no editing shared code to flip a runner) without churning every dedup/tokenize/download module, and the env var is opt-in (default behavior unchanged). Happy to implement Option B instead, or a hybrid (env var now + plumb through specific high-traffic entry points later).

Which would you like? Holding off on a PR until you confirm.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: great! minimal speed difference. I am hoping the total grad norm can start arching downwards before we make the swap, but probably fine either way.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I think swap to 16k context length will make the most sense, since its similar speed at 4k. Then when we want to do the first cooldown we can jump to 65k, another 4x gain. 4x jump per extension is on the more conservative side in literature. So I don't think we need to stick with 2x. Then another 4x to 262k at the very end of training.

On the 67B MoE we saw context extension 8k->65k at 20 percent into the run occur fine, with a grad spike in the first 10 steps but no loss spike. So it should be fine to swap when LR is still higher at 50 percent into the run.

The decision point during the swap is how we modify qk_mult. I think it is worth trying a couple options for 100 steps each w/ an eval at the end of each to empirically inform the decision. Deepseek empirically found their own optimal coef for MLA. The options are 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1) -> 1.48, or 1.3 × (0.1 × ln(4) + 1)^2 -> 1.68, or we take the midpoint at 1.58. Then we with whichever shows the lowest paloma macro and uncheatable eval loss. 

It is a little surprising that the total grad norm hasn't started going down on the hero run at 47 percent in. Though it looks stable enough to not be concerning. - if we were to see substantial continual grad norm rise after swap during 100 step test, then we could consider holding off on context extension until LR is at lower position 60-80 percent into the run.

The main reason for doing the context length increase now instead of later would be to enable the earlier cooldown to have a longer window at higher context, which is particularly relevant because the current plan is to use that earlier cooldown for RL'ing experts for the first pass of the final model.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Context-switch inventory, independently audited across data/resume, schedules/model settings, and eval/metrics against `main` at `3daf065582`. This revises the earlier inventory: **constant tokens per update preserves the schedules, but does not preserve the exact data stream**. The list below states implementation requirements and deployment prerequisites. The implementation is in draft PR [#9639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9639), rebuilt as three commits after independent xhigh code review and lint review; no review findings remain. Formatting/type checks pass, 135 targeted tests pass, and 2,901 selected tests pass. Twelve selected-suite failures and one focused checkpoint timeout reproduce on the base revision. Accelerator rehearsal and live cutover have not been performed.

**Schedules and model configuration**

- Keep the production update at **46,137,344 tokens**: batch 11264 at 4096, 5632 at 8192, or 2816 at 16384. Pass the actual context into both the model and optimizer heuristic. This preserves the 390251-step schedule, MuonH/Adam learning rates, beta2, epsilon, warmup/decay/cooldown fractions, and gate/router weight-decay annealing. Changing only batch or only the model silently changes these quantities. The weight-decay schedule reads the restored Adam count; restore the full optimizer state.
- Preserve the existing zero-based `run_progress = global_step / 390251` convention. Bounded diagnostics currently use their early stop as the denominator; fix them to use the full schedule. Grafana ETA depends on the existing convention. Watch, GC, eval, and checkpoint step cadences remain valid at constant tokens/update; checkpoint wall-clock cadence still follows elapsed time.
- Make context length, QK multiplier, and receiver capacity explicit launch settings. The current QK scalar applies to both local and global layers. The discussion proposes 16K trials at approximately 1.48, 1.58, and 1.68; choosing a winner requires evaluation. Global-only scaling would be an additional model change, not an existing option. Do not hardcode unmeasured QK/capacity choices into a phase table.
- Model and optimizer arrays have no batch/context-shaped leaves. Restore uses the new static model configuration with the old parameter/optimizer arrays and counters. A real save/resume rehearsal must still exercise the new compiled shapes, expert routing, and attention kernels. Local RoPE remains at the 2048 window; longer global attention changes FLOPs and memory.

**Data order and resume**

- The loader has no checkpointed cursor: it seeks by global step and batch schedule. Use a constant new sequence batch on relaunch. A historical sequence-batch schedule mixing 4K and 16K units does not represent token history correctly. Rebuild the datasets and loader at the new context length.
- Set `BlockShuffleConfig(io_block_size=2**20 // seq_len, window_blocks=512, perm_type="feistel")` for the Harrier mixture. It matches the old default at 4K and preserves the outer permutation of 1Mi-token blocks and complete 512Mi-token windows at longer contexts. **It does not preserve within-window order.** Keep the seed, component order, immutable token store, and shuffle policy fixed.
- The previous 17B-token estimate was a simulation result, not a general repeat bound. Each of 200 cells can have an in-progress 512Mi-token window: their combined window size is about 107.4B tokens. Per-cell mixture cursor shifts and truncated dataset tails are separate effects. The earlier naive-relaunch estimates (2.85T repeated and 1.6T unique tokens missed) have not been independently reproduced; use them as motivation, not a correctness guarantee.
- **Retain the 49152-sequence mixture blocks.** Shrinking them with context length changes floor-rounded per-cell weights and the remainder assigned to the largest cell. A calculation with the checked-in weights at step 195125 gives about 108.9B tokens of aggregate absolute complete-block cursor shift at 16K if the blocks are shrunk.
- With unchanged mixture blocks, the main/cooldown stage starts are 108000/312192 at 4K and 8K, 108096/312192 at 16K, and 108288/311808 at 64K. The previous inventory estimated 2.95B tokens of aggregate per-cell cursor displacement for the 4K→16K change with unchanged mixture blocks and the 108000→108096 historical boundary; that numerical estimate has not been independently reproduced. Require explicit acceptance when a continuation shifts these boundaries. Do not assert identical per-cell token blocks in the acceptance gate.

**Metrics and evaluation**

- `throughput/total_tokens` remains exact at the same completed step when tokens/update stays fixed. A one-rack rehearsal using fewer actual tokens/update has different data offsets and cumulative tokens even if its optimizer uses the production token budget.
- Cumulative `total_gflops` currently reprices all past updates using the new context. Supply a verified cumulative-FLOP baseline at the completed handoff step; add the new phase's cost after that boundary, retaining the baseline on retries. At boundary N, use the parent total after N completed updates (normally logged at global step N−1). Per-step MFU should use the new FLOP cost; compare speed using tokens/s and elapsed iteration time.
- Pin canonical `eval_dropless/*` evaluation to **4K packing** so inherited parent rows and the `eval_regressed` alert compare the same packing. Run 16K evaluation under a distinct prefix in the trial. Fixed packing does not isolate the effect of training context when QK also changes: record QK and use matched-QK controls when attributing gains.
- Run evaluation after the first resumed update, with deduplication when the periodic/final hook hits the same step. The old first-step hook fires only at global update 1, otherwise the first new-context evaluation can wait until the next 3000-step boundary. Dropless evaluation must emit the watchdog's evaluation lifecycle events. Rehearse train → eval → next train, including dropless memory, before deployment.

**Rehearsal and acceptance**

1. CPU regression checks: compare 4K/8K/16K schedules and optimizer updates from restored counters; verify constant token totals, fixed shuffle-window coverage, documented mixture boundaries, fixed eval packing, resumed eval cadence, and cumulative FLOPs across retry. Exact optimizer/schedule equality is appropriate; exact shuffled batches and equal loss are not.
2. Restore the actual handoff checkpoint on one rack: use a 4K/QK1.3 control and 16K arms at QK1.48,1.58,1.68, each for 2–3 seeds × 200 steps. Add 4K controls at matching QK values if attributing a gain specifically to training context. Use `schedule_steps=390251`, production optimizer tokens/update, and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The original diagnostics used a smaller optimizer budget and zero gate/router decay. Smaller execution batches still change gradient statistics and data position; this is a rehearsal, not a production-equivalent gradient comparison.
3. Measure loss offset/drift, grad norm, router/drop metrics, tokens/s, iteration time, and peak memory. Include a dropless evaluation at each required packing and a save/resume. Record replacement acceptance/rollback thresholds for loss drift, gradient spikes, expert drops, throughput, and memory from these arms before authorizing deployment. The earlier measured context-dependent loss offsets mean the normal same-objective paired-loss gate cannot be applied unchanged.
4. During the production trial, verify LR, Adam LR, progress, token totals, mixture stage/weights, and FLOP continuity at matching completed steps. Compare windowed loss/gradient/drop/throughput statistics with the rehearsal bands. Score parent and child checkpoints on fixed held-out Paloma and uncheatable sets at both packings; keep short-context retention and long-context quality separate.

**Handoff record and remaining decisions**

Update the run ID, complete durable checkpoint, W&B fork point, source SHA, context/batch/QK/capacity, eval policy, FLOP baseline, mixture-shift acceptance, and rollback command together. The trigger should validate the child tracker has the same settings on retries and record them in #8506. Check checkpoint metadata, region-local storage headroom, and retention before the cutover. An old binary without requested permanent saves needs a forced temporary checkpoint copied to a durable prefix before pruning; each full hero copy was estimated at 4.29 TB in the earlier inventory. The previous live step/ETA is stale and must be refreshed at deployment.

Open deployment decisions: final QK and capacity, explicit acceptance of the 16K data shift, empirical trial thresholds, and the handoff checkpoint/time. A 64K or 262K phase also needs its own batch/mesh/attention and memory validation. The changes described here do not establish those later deployments as ready.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
> Wonder if its possible to do a clean handoff point as long as our checkpoint lands on a step that is divisible by the right number.

@ClassicLarry I've been looking into this, and it seems pretty tricky to resume with a different context length without repeating or dropping tokens. It seems like there are at least 4 independent sources of potential misalignment:

1. Levanter currently splits sources into "shuffle blocks" of 256 sequences and then the blocks are permuted. When we change the sequence length, the block sizes also change and the permuted sequence differs. So even if we restart the run at a shuffle block boundary, we'll inevitably drop and repeat tokens. #9689 fixes this by setting the tokens per shuffle block to ~1M (the current value, with 4k context), independently of the context size.
2. In addition to the block-level permutation above, we also permute _sequences_ within 512-block windows. When we change the sequence length, we change the result of permutation. (Note, we can't just work around this by doing the handoff at a step divisible by some number, since each source is at a different point in its window, and the rate at which tokens are consumed from a source is determined by its mixture weight). This seems like the largest effect after (1) and also the hardest to work around.
3. The token stream is divided into "mixture blocks" of 49152 sequences. To avoid dropping/repeating tokens, we need to hand off at a mixture block boundary. For a given batch size, mixture block boundaries coincide with steps every `49152 / gcd(49152, B)` steps. At C=16k, B=2816, this is 192 steps.
4. The data mix has a stage start at 108k. But mixture stages must fall on steps that are also mixture block boundaries, which are multiples of 192 steps at batch size 2816 (what we'd use with 16k context). We could either move the stage start to 108096 or 107904; the former skips some tokens from sources whose weight decreased at the switch and repeats some tokens from sources whose weight increased; the latter vice-versa.

One option is to merge #9689 to fix (1), hand off at the 216k permanent checkpoint to avoid (3), and accept the drops/repeats due to (2) and (4). I'm a bit hesitant, though - it seems like this has the potential to drop/repeat 10s of billions of tokens.

Wondering if we should instead look into an adhoc patch, something like finishing each source's current window in the order the 4k run was using before switching to 16k? This seems like it could get quite messy, though, and I'm hesitant to pursue it unless we think it's really necessary.

@ravwojdyla @Helw150 curious for your thoughts here as well. How did we manage this for the 67B run?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Proposal: a clean context-length handoff** (replying to @mcwitt's four misalignment points above)

1. Fix shuffle blocks at ~1M tokens, so the level-1 block permutation is the same at every seq_len (#9689).
2. Give each data-mix stage its own `seq_len` and `batch_size`, e.g. `(216000, mix2, seq_len=16384, B=2816)`. A stage then only has to land on a mixture-block boundary in its own units, which fixes points 3 and 4.
3. Track each source's read position in **tokens** carried across stages, instead of in sequences of a single length.
4. On a `seq_len` change, advance each source to its next shuffle-window boundary (skip-to-window). Nothing repeats; only the unread rest of each source's current window is skipped, which fixes point 2. Using `harrier_mix_2026_08_18` at a 216k handoff, that is about **52B unseen tokens** across 200 sources, ≈0.26B each and ~0.6% of the remaining run.
5. Inside a stage, mixing, batching and BOS/EOS/segment handling are unchanged.

Finishing the partially read windows instead would serve leftover 4k slices glued into 16k sequences. Those need segment and loss masking at the joins, carry only 4k of context, and low-weight sources would keep serving them for thousands of steps after the switch. So skip-to-window looks like the better trade-off.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Thanks for the thorough investigation! The 67B would have had some reshuffling on its context length change, I did not account for all levels of the shuffle there.

I am in favor of skipping ahead to each data bucket's next 512-block window. So at most a data bucket will skip 512x256x4096 = 500 million tokens. I cant think of a clean way around this.

comments.body:

We will face this challenge again when we go to 65k. So perhaps we should have the code permute sequences at 65k now, then chop up at 16k.

That'll make our shuffle logic context size independent for the rest of the run (and I agree skip the rest of the current block for everything here).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> For the hero, we already shuffled the data globally in Datakit, so we could keep a fixed token-sized I/O block shuffle and drop the inner sequence shuffle. That'll make our shuffle logic context size independent for the rest of the run (and I agree skip the rest of the current block for everything here).

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body: Long term, we should add `seq_len` to `BatchSchedule`. For each shuffle window, shuffle at the largest context length used while consuming it, then split into smaller sequences as scheduled. With divisible lengths and transitions aligned to those larger units, this preserves data order across context changes without requiring a globally shuffled store.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body: The inner shuffle was mainly intended to make it so that you didn't need to globally shuffle at write time and so you can test variance from different global shuffles w/o storing write copies.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
@ravwojdyla and I just chatted. I'm probs over-engineering above.

We should just skip the rest of each source's current shuffle window whenever we change `seq_len`. It's the lowest-risk option: it preserves the shuffle behavior that's been working so far, at a small cost (50B tokens worst case). Those tokens will come back around if we exhaust a bucket; otherwise, we'll use fresh tokens in their place.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Prompt completions across three permanent checkpoints — **step-6000, step-24000, step-42000** — sampled at temperature 0.2. Each prompt is sampled independently (own batch row, own position) in one forward per step; `⟨EOS⟩` = ended naturally, `⟨cut at max_new_tokens⟩` = hit the 200-token cap. Two prompt sets: code/open-ended (seed 0) and factual lists (seed 1).

## Code / open-ended prompts (temp 0.2, seed 0)

### `def add_two_numbers(x, y):`
_(temp 0.2)_

**6k** ⟨cut at max_new_tokens⟩
```
def add_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x + y  

def subtract_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x - y  

def multiply_two_numbers(x, y):  
    return x * y  

def divide_two_numbers(x, y):

        raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero.")
```
